name: Micropigmentation / scar tattooing

lead: Micropigmentation, also called paramedical tattooing or permanent makeup, places pigment matched to your surrounding skin into a scar so the contrast shrinks and the scar blends in. The colour change is visible once the pigment is placed.

Encyclopedia references list scar covering, vitiligo camouflage, nipple-areola reconstruction after mastectomy and eyebrow restoration among its medical uses. No clinical studies specific to appearance outcomes were identified.

paras: A trained practitioner deposits the pigment in a clinic or studio, often in more than one session, matching colour to the surrounding skin. It is raised in looksmaxxing discussions mainly for pale or discolored scars.
Tattoos are long-lasting. Conditions that impair wound healing, such as diabetes, may affect choices about location and timing.

angle.text: Micropigmentation tattoos skin-matched pigment into pale or discolored scars so they blend with the skin around them, and the change shows as soon as the pigment is placed. It is established in medical use for scar covering and vitiligo, with little formal outcome data.

lead: Micropigmentation, also called permanent makeup, medical tattooing or paramedical tattooing, deposits pigment into the dermis to reduce how visible scars and pigment differences are. People use it to blend pale or discoloured scars into the surrounding skin tone, to fill in patches of lost colour such as stable vitiligo, to restore eyebrows, and to re-create an areola after breast surgery, so the area reads as natural skin from normal viewing distance.[1][2][3]

A 2023 review in the Indian Dermatology Online Journal describes micropigmentation and microblading as a popular semi-permanent camouflage technique for stable vitiligo, androgenetic or stable alopecia areata, and semi-permanent makeup, and says knowledge of colour theory is central to a natural result.[3] Wikipedia describes paramedical tattoos as realistic-style tattoos meant to conceal a medical condition or the results of its treatment.[1]
In looksmaxxing discussions the same technique appears mostly in its scalp form, where dots of pigment mimic closely cropped hair to conceal thinning or surgical scarring.[4][5]

paras: Medical or paramedical tattoos can conceal scars or treatment effects, recreate a nipple and areola after mastectomy or fill pigment loss after reduction surgery with a free nipple graft, and reduce the visibility of vitiligo patches.[1] Tattoos have also been used to restore eyebrows in conditions such as alopecia.[1] Permanent makeup covers a wider set of cosmetic procedures, including eyebrows, eyeliner, lip colour, burn and scar camouflage, and scalp tattooing.[2]

Scalp micropigmentation conceals alopecia by depositing permanent pigment between follicles in a stippling pattern resembling closely cut hair; a clinicopathologic case report describes evenly spaced grey to black dots on trichoscopy.[4] The 2023 micropigmentation review lists androgenetic alopecia and stable alopecia areata among its indications.[3]

Tattooing for medical purposes goes back centuries: Galen attempted corneal tattooing around 150 CE, a German doctor used mercury sulfide and white lead over skin lesions in 1835, and tattooing of scarred lips began in 1911.[1] In cosmetic practice, the London tattooist Sutherland MacDonald is the most widely documented early practitioner of permanent makeup, in 1902, and George Burchett developed the technique further in the 1930s.[2]

Wikipedia notes that skin tone influences how a given pigment looks, that sun exposure and lifestyle can fade tattoos, and that people should have realistic expectations.[2] Because diabetes can impair wound healing, people with diabetes may need to consider location and timing of a medical tattoo.[1]

No studies found of scar tattooing specifically for appearance outcomes. Review-level literature describes micropigmentation as a camouflage method for stable vitiligo, alopecia and semi-permanent makeup,[3] and a 2010 Cochrane review notes that most vitiligo treatments available are largely unsatisfactory.[6]

In a study of permanent makeup complications, the most common effects were itching, redness and occasional swelling that healed within days; uncommon complications include allergic reaction to pigment, infection, granulomas, keloids and bleeding.[2] Pigment placed too deep can migrate and blur, and removal by laser, dermabrasion or surgery can be difficult or impossible.[2] Rare swelling or burning during MRI has been reported, mostly linked to poor-quality or metal-adulterated pigments.[2] In the US, inks are subject to FDA approval as cosmetics, though regulation of pigments is described as loose.[2]

claims.claim: Scalp micropigmentation suits only certain people, such as those who keep a buzzed look or have diffuse thinning or surgical scarring
